title: Animal Camouflage
keyIdea: Camouflage is when an animal's colour or pattern helps it blend in with its habitat, so it is hard to see. Prey animals use camouflage to hide from predators, and predators use it to creep up on their prey. Camouflage only works on the right background: a white hare is hidden on snow but stands out on brown earth. Stripes and spots can also break up an animal's outline.

kid: Some animals are hard to see. Their colour or pattern looks like the place where they live. This is called camouflage.
A green caterpillar on a green leaf blends in. A bird looking for food may not see it. A red caterpillar stands out.
Camouflage needs the right background. A white hare hides on snow. On brown mud, the same white hare is easy to spot.
Hunters hide too. A tiger's stripes look like long grass and shadows. It can creep up close to a deer.
adult: In England's Year 2 science, children learn that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited. In Year 6 this becomes adaptation. Camouflage is one of the first adaptations children meet. It means colours, patterns or shapes that make an animal hard to tell apart from its background.

Prey such as moths, caterpillars and hares use camouflage to avoid predators. Predators such as tigers, polar bears and snow leopards use it to get close to prey. Some animals change with the seasons: the mountain hare grows a white coat in winter and a brown one in summer. Stripes and spots work by breaking up the outline, which is called disruptive colouring.

Common mistakes: children often think an animal hides because it is small or keeps still, and miss that the match with the background is the key. Many think white always hides, when it only hides on a pale background. Others think only prey animals use camouflage. Be careful with bright animals like ladybirds: they stand out on purpose, as a warning that they taste bad.

In the lab your child taps the caterpillar a bird would find last, colours a moth to match bark, drags a white hare from brown earth onto snow, and picks the coat that hides a tiger in grass. Last, they watch a bird hunt moths on bark and see that only the brown ones are left.

familyTip: On a walk, look for animals and insects that are hard to spot, such as a moth on a tree trunk or a frog in the grass. Ask: what colour is it, and what colour is the place it lives? Play hide and seek with a few coloured toys on a rug or in the garden: which ones are found first?

practice.prompt: A brown moth rests on brown tree bark. Why is it hard for a bird to see?
practice.hint: Look at the colour of the moth and the colour of the bark.
practice.explain: Brown on brown blends in. That is camouflage. Being small or still helps a little, but the colour match is the main reason.

practice.prompt: There are {a} moths on brown bark. {b} of them are brown. A bird eats every moth that is not brown. How many moths are left?
practice.hint: Which moths does the bird not see? Count only those.
practice.explain: The bird finds the {=a-b} moths that stand out. The {b} brown moths blend in, so {b} moths are left.

practice.prompt: A bird sees {a} red caterpillars and {b} green caterpillars on green leaves. It can only spot the red ones. How many caterpillars does it spot?
practice.hint: The green ones blend in with the leaves.
practice.explain: Only the red caterpillars stand out, so the bird spots {a}. The {b} green ones are camouflaged.

practice.prompt: Where is a white hare hidden best?
practice.hint: White blends in with something that is also white.
practice.explain: White on white blends in, so snow hides a white hare. On mud or grass the white coat stands out.

choices: colours or patterns that help an animal blend in
pool.hint: Think of a green frog on a green leaf.
pool.explain: Camouflage is a colour, pattern or shape that makes an animal hard to see against its background. Running fast or hiding in a hole are other ways to stay safe.

pool.prompt: Why does a polar bear have white-looking fur?
choices: to blend in with snow and ice
so seals can see it coming
pool.hint: Where does a polar bear live and hunt?
pool.explain: White fur blends in with snow and ice, so a polar bear can get close to seals without being seen.

pool.prompt: A tiger hides in long grass to catch a deer. Who is using camouflage?
pool.hint: A predator hunts. Which animal here is hiding so it can creep close?
pool.explain: The tiger is the predator. Its stripes look like grass and shadow, so it can creep close to its prey.

pool.prompt: Which moth will a bird find first on brown bark?
choices: they are all found at the same time
pool.hint: Which colour stands out on brown?
pool.explain: Yellow stands out on brown bark, so the bird finds it first. The brown moth blends in and is found last.

pool.prompt: How do a tiger's stripes help it hide?
choices: they break up its shape so it looks like grass
pool.hint: Look at the shape you can see in long grass.
pool.explain: Dark stripes look like the shadows between grass, so the tiger's outline is hard to see.

pool.prompt: A mountain hare is white in winter. What colour is it in summer, when the snow has gone?
pool.hint: What colour is the ground in summer?
pool.explain: In summer it grows a brown coat, so it blends in with the earth and rocks. Staying white would make it stand out.

pool.prompt: {a} frogs sit on a green leaf. {b} of them are green and the rest are yellow. How many frogs stand out?
pool.hint: Which frogs do not match the leaf? Take the green ones away.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}, so {=a-b} yellow frogs stand out. The {b} green frogs blend in.

pool.prompt: A bird hunts on snow. There are {a} white hares and {b} brown hares. The bird spots only the brown ones. How many hares stay hidden?
pool.explain: The {a} white hares blend in with the snow, so {a} stay hidden. The {b} brown hares stand out.
